entities.name: Tudor period
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Tudor Dynasty of England (1485–1603), founded when Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth Field and became Henry VII, was arguably the most consequential dynasty in English history — encompassing the English Reformation, the break with Rome, the dissolution of the monasteries, the Elizabethan literary and musical renaissance, the beginning of British global exploration, and the Protestant-Catholic religious wars that shaped British identity for 400 years. Five Tudors governed a century that transformed England from a medieval Catholic kingdom to a Protestant nation-state.

Henry VII (1485-1509) ended the Wars of the Roses and stabilized English finances. Henry VIII (1509-1547) broke with Rome (1534) to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, dissolved over 800 monasteries, executed two wives and two chancellors, and created the Church of England — a theological and political revolution that established English Protestantism. Edward VI's brief Protestant radicalism was followed by 'Bloody Mary' (Mary I) burning 300 Protestants before Elizabeth I's 45-year reign created England's golden age.

Elizabeth I's reign (1558-1603) produced Shakespeare, Marlowe, and Spenser; Drake's circumnavigation; Raleigh's Virginia expeditions; the Armada defeat; and the creation of a Protestant English national identity. The Tudor century created most of the institutions — Parliament's independence, common law courts, English Bible, Church of England — that became the foundation of English constitutionalism exported to America, Australia, and India through the British Empire.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Tudor Dynasty created the Church of England, dissolved the monasteries, produced Shakespeare, and established the Protestant English national identity — a century of transformation that shaped the British constitutional tradition exported via empire to a billion people.
